## Q1 | Malodorous Byproducts

Butterbeer is beloved by Hogwarts students and teachers alike and is widely available at wizarding shops. But the beverage has the negative effect of generating displeasing odors from its imbibers. Model the private market for butterbeer using private and social cost and benefit curves. Indicate on your graph the private equilibrium quantity and social equilibrium quantity.

Preferences for butterbeer and its marginal cost can be represented by the following relationships.

$$
D: P_B = 100 - \frac{1}{2} Q_D \qquad\qquad S: P_S = 20 + \frac{1}{2} Q_S
$$

Prices are in galleons and quantity is in bottles. The odor imposes a cost of 20 galleons per bottle on everyone nearby.

::::: solution

Marginal Social Cost: $P = 40 + \frac{1}{2} Q$. Market Equilibrium Price: $60$ galleons. Market Equilibrium Quantity: $80$ bottles. Socially Efficient Quantity: $60$ bottles. Deadweight Loss: $200$ galleons.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Demand is the marginal private benefit (MPB) and supply is the marginal private cost (MPC). The odor adds $20$ of cost to every bottle, borne by people nearby, so the marginal social cost sits $20$ above supply:

$$
\text{MSC} = (20 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q) + 20 = 40 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q
$$

The market ignores the odor, so it clears where demand meets supply:

$$
100 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 20 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 80, \quad P = 60
$$

The efficient quantity counts the odor, so demand meets MSC:

$$
100 - \tfrac{1}{2} Q = 40 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 60, \quad P = 70
$$

:::

::: column

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

Bottles $61$ through $80$ cost society more (MSC) than buyers value them (MPB), yet the market makes them. The deadweight loss is the triangle between MSC and demand over those $20$ bottles. Its height at $Q = 80$ is $\text{MSC} - \text{MPB} = 80 - 60 = 20$:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times (80 - 60) = 200
$$

:::::

## Q2 | Covid Vaccine

Lets model Covid and assume the following.

1. There is a linear marginal private benefit curve for the vaccine.
2. The vaccine carries with it a positive externality.
3. There is a linear upward sloping supply curve for the vaccine. The supply curve for the vaccine is a little funny, and we’ll talk about imperfect close substitutes in the next few weeks. But we’ll just assume it’s there.

Use a graph to discuss the welfare in the market and any potential market failure.

The graph below shows the market. The upper downward-sloping curve is marginal social benefit and the lower one is marginal private benefit. Supply is both the private and the social cost. The lettered regions are for the questions.

![Covid vaccine market with MPB, MSB and S, and regions A, B and C](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=30%}

Market Quantity ($\hat{Q}$):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

Socially Efficient Quantity ($Q^*$):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

::::

:::: {.columns .continued gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=30%}

Deadweight Loss region (letter):

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

:::

::: {.column width=30%}

:::

::: {.column width=20%}

:::

::::

::::: solution

Market Quantity: $40$ vaccinations. Socially Efficient Quantity: $50$ vaccinations. Deadweight Loss region: B.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

Buyers weigh only their own benefit, so the market clears where MPB meets supply. On the graph MPB is $P = 100 - Q$ and supply is $P = 20 + Q$:

$$
100 - Q = 20 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 40, \quad P = 60
$$

The efficient quantity counts the benefit to everyone else, so MSB, $P = 120 - Q$, meets supply:

$$
120 - Q = 20 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 50, \quad P = 70
$$

The vaccinations from $40$ to $50$ are worth more to society (MSB) than they cost (S), but they never happen. The lost surplus is the triangle between MSB and supply over those units: region B, worth $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 10 = 100$.

Region A is the external benefit the first $40$ vaccinations already give to others; it is gained, not lost. Region C lies below supply, under cost, so it is not surplus at all.

:::

::: column

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

:::::

Why does the market provide too few vaccinations?

> a\) Each vaccination costs society more to produce than it costs the seller.
>
> b\) Each vaccination is worth more to society than to the person buying it, so at the market quantity marginal social benefit is still above marginal cost.
>
> c\) Buyers value each vaccination less than sellers’ marginal cost, so too few buyers enter the market.
>
> d\) The market quantity is already socially efficient, so no vaccinations are missing.

::: solution

**b)**

The person getting vaccinated also protects the people around them, but does not count that benefit when deciding. At the market quantity of $40$, MSB is $80$ while marginal cost is only $60$, so one more vaccination would add $20$ of surplus. a) describes an external cost, the butterbeer story, not this one. c) is wrong because at $Q = 40$ the buyer’s value equals marginal cost; buyers are not underpaying, they are leaving out others’ benefit. d) is wrong because the market stops $10$ short of the efficient $50$.

:::
